doc.title: Eddie Marshall interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 8, 2002

title: Writing process, Hutcherson as theory teacher, recorder suite
summary: He now starts from chord progressions, learned voicings from his father and Bobby Hutcherson, and plans a Baroque-flavored recorder suite.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Does a tune usually start with the recorder?

Sometimes it starts — it the early days it started with the recorder. Now it starts a lot, mostly with chord progressions a lot of the times. I got into theory and harmony with a lot of different musicians. First with my dad, you know, I did want to know what he was doing. I was a piano player too for a while, you know, I took piano lessons and stuff. And I’ve always messed around with the piano. But voicings have always fascinated me. You know I remember the first time someone showed me how to do alternate voices, it was just like one-three-five and then he’d go three-five-one or five-three — you know. And that just led, the voicings. And then I started playing with Bobby Hutcherson, who was like — actually I’d have to say he was my theory teacher and still is. Because he is just so knowledgeable and always so willing to show me how these chords move and how this scale goes with that you know, and stuff I would never learn if I went to school. Because he always was patient. And I would go back and try this and then write. And I still have a lot of stuff that I wrote twenty years ago, thirty years ago. And now I use the computer. I’m computerized. So now I’m writing this piece, I’m trying to get grants. I still love to write jazz pieces but now I’m writing on, I got sort of interested in Baroque music in the last twenty years or so. And I’m writing this music for two tenor recorders, oboe and © Fillius Jazz Archive -16-

cello. And it’s going to be — I’m trying to get a grant to do this. And it’s going to be a suite. And then on some of the pieces I’m going to add like percussion, bass and piano. And I’m really excited about this because this is the first time I’ve done something like this.
Sounds like an interesting combination of sounds.

Yeah. And it really sounds good. It’s different, and the venues I’m choosing to do it in, like in San Francisco they have a lot of functions at churches, some of the old wooden churches. There’s a church here in the city called Old First Church where they do concerts with small ensembles and stuff like that.
